content: 1. Allocation concealment was unclear in three trials, and outcome assessors were not blinded in two trials, leading to a single downgrade in the assessment of risk of bias. Additionally, three trials did not adequately describe incomplete outcome data or the intention-to-treat analysis. 2. Risk of bias was downgraded once because allocation concealment was unclear in three trials, and outcome assessors were not blinded in three trials. In one trial, incomplete data were not adequately described, and in another, the analysis did not follow the intention-to-treat principle. 3. Risk of bias was downgraded once due to unclear allocation concealment in two trials and lack of blinding of outcome assessors in another two trials. Four trials reported incomplete data and did not perform the final analysis based on the intention-to-treat principle. 4. Risk of bias was downgraded once because allocation concealment was unclear, and the outcome assessor was not blinded in one trial. 5. Imprecision was downgraded once due to a small sample size. 6. Risk of bias was downgraded once because allocation concealment was unclear in one trial, and outcome assessors were not blinded in two trials. 7. Imprecision was downgraded once because the sample size was smaller than 200 participants. 8. Indirectness was downgraded once because the comparison groups were not identical. 9. Imprecision was downgraded once due to a wide confidence interval for the treatment effect. 10. Risk of bias was downgraded once because allocation concealment and the procedure for masking the outcome assessor were unclear in one trial, and the outcome assessor was not blinded in another trial. 11. Imprecision was downgraded once due to a small sample size (fewer than 200 participants). 12. Risk of bias was downgraded once because allocation was not concealed in one trial and was unclear in another two trials. The procedure for masking the outcome assessor was not adequately described in two trials, and information on incomplete data was unclear in three trials. 13. Risk of bias was downgraded once because allocation was not concealed in two trials and was unclear in another two trials. Outcome assessors were not blinded in two trials. 14. Imprecision was downgraded once due to a small sample size (fewer than 200 participants). 15. The majority of available studies were conducted in high-income countries, with few trials focusing specifically on older people living in the community. This may explain the relatively modest effect sizes observed. More research is needed to explore the effects of nutritional interventions beyond supplementation for this specific group. 16. In many lowand middle-income countries, nutritional interventions are delivered by non-specialist healthcare workers for undernourished children and pregnant mothers. Based on existing practice, suitably trained non-specialist healthcare workers can effectively deliver nutritional interventions to older people at risk of undernutrition or undernourishment. 17. Promoting nutritional interventions for older people will increase equity in healthcare. 18. The GDG strongly believes that this recommendation will improve equity in health. 19. Oral supplemental nutrition with dietary advice should be recommended for older people affected by undernutrition. The quality of evidence is moderate, and the strength of the recommendation is strong. 20. Dietary advice as a stand-alone intervention received no recommendation due to limited evidence on its effectiveness among older people at risk of undernutrition or undernourishment. 21. The policy priority to support nutritional outcomes among older people must focus on food quality, diversity, and nutrition security. 22. Nutritional supplements administered aimed to provide between an additional 97 kcal per day and a maximum of 1200 kcal per day. Most trials administered supplements with 20 g or more of protein per day, often including micronutrients. 23. The duration of nutritional interventions ranged from 10 days to 6 months in trials conducted in hospital and long-term care settings. In community settings, the duration ranged from 3 months to 18 months. 24. Specially formulated supplementary foods—modified in energy density, protein, fat, or micronutrient composition—should be encouraged to meet the nutritional requirements of older people. 25. Physical, functional, psychological, and social factors predisposing older people to undernutrition should be identified and addressed. 26. Careful assessment of undernutrition—including functional, anthropometric, biochemical, and clinical assessments—should be considered by trained healthcare professionals for older people at risk of or suspected of undernutrition. 27. Nutrition assessment should be an integral part of primary care for older people. 28. A social environment that promotes increased food intake for older people with or at risk of undernutrition should be encouraged. 29. Encouraging all older people at risk of undernutrition to consume oral nutritional supplements (particularly in liquid or powder form) may be unacceptable in some communities. Other strategies, such as dietary advice or nutritional education programs, could be considered. 30. Although there is no direct evidence for the benefit of dietary advice, guidance on measures to supplement the caloric content in a normal diet should be encouraged when possible. 31. The older person’s tastes and preferences should be considered when administering oral nutritional supplements to improve adherence. 32. Greater research and clarity are required to determine the best quality and quantity of oral nutritional supplementation. 33. The limited number of studies from lowand middle-income countries means generalizability warrants consideration. 34. The GDG decided not to issue a stand-alone recommendation for mealtime interventions (including family-style meals and social dining) due to the generic nature of the intervention.
